core: Order of magnitude as the power of ten of a quantity; why a result good to a factor of two or three is often decisive early in design
Decomposition: breaking an unknown into factors that can each be bounded
The Fermi-problem method and its documented history (Fermi's Trinity paper-scrap estimate)
Bounding by upper and lower limits and squeezing; the geometric mean of wide bounds
Sanity checks by dimensional analysis and by comparison with a known reference quantity
How errors behave when independent estimates are multiplied: RMS growth like sqrt(n) rather than worst case, and the failure of that argument when errors are correlated
A dozen reference quantities worth knowing by heart, with correct values and units
Engineering payoff: rejecting infeasible concepts, sizing systems, checking computed or simulated results
Professional obligation to label an estimate as an estimate and record its assumptions
supporting: Worked Fermi estimate: mass of Earth's atmosphere from surface pressure, compared with Trenberth and Smith (2005)
Worked Fermi estimate: annual U.S. motor gasoline consumption, compared with EIA data
GAO cost-estimating practice as a documented professional standard for recording ground rules and assumptions
outOfScope: SI base units, unit conversion procedure, and significant-figure rules (owned by engineering-fundamentals:engineering-thinking:units-measurement-and-significant-figures)
Formal measurement uncertainty budgets, Type A/Type B evaluation, and coverage factors
Statistical inference, confidence intervals, and regression
Any design value, allowable stress, or load factor from a governing code

claims.claim: The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of ten nearest its value, and an order-of-magnitude estimate is normally carried to one significant figure; the working goal is to land in the right ballpark rather than to be precise.

Standard estimation strategies include building large lengths from small ones, getting areas and volumes from estimated lengths, getting masses from volumes and approximate densities, and bounding an unfamiliar quantity between an upper and a lower limit and taking the geometric mean.

At the Trinity test on 16 July 1945 Enrico Fermi estimated the yield by dropping small pieces of paper into the blast wave and observing their horizontal displacement, arriving at roughly 10 kilotons of TNT equivalent.

The long-standing U.S. Department of Energy yield figure for Trinity is 21 kilotons; a 2021 radiochemical reassessment of trinitite samples by Los Alamos researchers gives 24.8 +/- 2 kilotons. Fermi's 10-kiloton figure is therefore low by a factor of about 2.1 to 2.5.
Fermi's method sensed only the blast wave, which does not carry the thermal and nuclear-radiation share of the energy release, so his figure is expected to be low rather than randomly wrong.
The standard acceleration of gravity is fixed by convention at 9.80665 m/s^2 (declared as 980.665 cm/s^2 by the 3rd CGPM in 1901).
The standard atmosphere is defined as exactly 101 325 newtons per square metre (1 013 250 dyn/cm^2), adopted by the 10th CGPM in 1954.

Useful density anchors: water at 4 degrees C is 1.000 x 10^3 kg/m^3, iron or steel about 7.8 x 10^3 kg/m^3, aluminium 2.7 x 10^3 kg/m^3, lead 11.3 x 10^3 kg/m^3, and air about 1.29 kg/m^3 at 0 degrees C and 101.3 kPa.
The thermochemical calorie is exactly 4.184 J and the thermochemical kilocalorie is exactly 4184 J, so a food Calorie (a kilocalorie) is about 4.2 kJ.

U.S. nutrition labelling uses a reference caloric intake of 2,000 calories per day for adults and children four years and older, and permits energy per serving to be shown in kilojoules alongside the calorie figure.
A 2,000 Calorie daily intake corresponds to a continuous metabolic power of about 97 W, which is why 10^2 W is the right order of magnitude for whole-body human power.
claims.note: Arithmetic executed in Bash: 2000 * 4184 J / 86400 s = 96.85 W.

claims.claim: Sustained mechanical power output for an elite cyclist is a few hundred watts: race data summarised in a narrative review indicate that a top male grand-tour general-classification contender must produce about 5.8 W/kg for 20 minutes on key mountain climbs, roughly 400 W for a 70 kg rider.
claims.note: The review attributes the 5.8 W/kg figure to van Erp et al. (2020). Arithmetic executed in Bash: 5.8 W/kg * 70 kg = 406 W.

claims.claim: The total mean mass of Earth's atmosphere is 5.1480 x 10^18 kg, and the global mean total surface pressure is 985.50 hPa, which is lower than the sea-level standard atmosphere because the mean solid surface sits above sea level.

A Fermi estimate of atmospheric mass as M = P*A/g with P = 1 x 10^5 Pa, R = 6.4 x 10^6 m and g = 10 m/s^2 gives 5.15 x 10^18 kg; treating Earth as a sphere of its equatorial radius (6.378 x 10^6 m, from NASA's 12 756 km equatorial diameter) with the exact standard atmosphere and standard gravity gives 5.28 x 10^18 kg, 2.6 percent above the published value, and substituting the global mean surface pressure of 985.50 hPa brings it to 5.14 x 10^18 kg, 0.2 percent below.
claims.note: All arithmetic executed in Bash. Earth radius taken as half the NASA-published equatorial diameter of 12 756 km; the spherical-equatorial assumption slightly overstates surface area because Earth is oblate, and this is stated in the lesson.

claims.claim: U.S. finished motor gasoline consumption averaged about 8.94 million barrels per day, or about 376 million gallons per day, in 2023; at 42 gallons per barrel that is roughly 1.4 x 10^11 gallons per year.
claims.note: Arithmetic executed in Bash: 8.94e6 bbl/d * 42 gal/bbl * 365 d = 1.371e11 gal/yr.

claims.claim: A four-factor Fermi estimate of U.S. annual gasoline use (3 x 10^8 people, two-thirds of them drivers, 10^4 miles each per year, 25 miles per gallon) gives 8.0 x 10^10 gallons per year, which is 0.58 times the EIA figure - the same order of magnitude, low by a factor of about 1.7.

For independent quantities the relative standard deviation of a product is the quadrature sum of the relative standard deviations of the factors; a covariance term must be added when the factors are not independent.

If four independent factors are each uncertain by up to a factor of two, the worst-case product error is a factor of 16, but simulation gives a root-mean-square error of only about a factor of 2.2; if instead every factor is biased in the same direction, the RMS error grows to about a factor of 5.0.
claims.note: Monte Carlo with 400,000 trials executed in Bash, seed 20260819; log10 errors drawn uniform on +/- log10(2) per factor. Matches the closed form RMS(log10) = halfwidth * sqrt(n/3) for the independent case.

claims.claim: GAO's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide names four characteristics of a reliable estimate - comprehensive, well documented, accurate, and credible - and devotes Step 5 of its twelve-step process to identifying ground rules and assumptions, stating that the most uncertain assumptions must be well documented for the estimate to be credible.
Engineering lessons of this kind are educational material, not engineering design guidance; real design work requires a licensed engineer working to the governing code.
claims.note: Project-level editorial requirement from the subject source map, not a sourced factual claim; the GAO id is attached only because it is the closest professional-practice reference in the packet.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The accepted yield of the Trinity test
positions: The long-published U.S. Department of Energy figure is 21 kilotons.
Selby et al. (2021), reanalysing trinitite by high-precision mass spectrometry at Los Alamos, report 24.8 +/- 2 kilotons.
Katz (2021) works against an accepted radiochemical value of 25 +/- 2 kilotons.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives both figures and states the comparison as a range: Fermi's 10 kilotons is low by a factor of roughly 2.1 (against 21 kt) to 2.5 (against 24.8 kt). No single number is asserted as the settled value.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which pressure to use when estimating atmospheric mass
positions: The sea-level standard atmosphere, 101 325 Pa, is the familiar anchor.
Trenberth and Smith (2005) report a global mean total surface pressure of 985.50 hPa, because the mean solid surface is above sea level.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the standard atmosphere for the estimate, reports the resulting 2.4 percent overshoot, and names the surface-elevation effect as the physical reason, showing the refined calculation as a check.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a rough Fermi pass that lands within a fraction of a percent should be reported as accurate
positions: The rounded pass (R = 6.4e6 m, P = 1e5 Pa, g = 10 m/s^2) returns 5.15e18 kg, within 0.02 percent of the published value.
The refined pass with exact constants is 2.4 percent high.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states explicitly that the rounded pass agrees so closely only because rounding errors happened to cancel, and that a Fermi estimate should never be reported to better precision than a factor of two regardless of how close it lands.

sourceRecords.notes: Confirms that order-of-magnitude estimates are carried to one significant figure, and that the conventional strategies are scaling lengths, deriving areas and volumes, converting volumes to masses with approximate densities, and bounding an unknown between limits and taking the geometric mean. Also supplies the coarse density anchors (air ~1 kg/m^3, water ~10^3 kg/m^3, dense solids ~10^4 kg/m^3). No wording reused.

sourceRecords.notes: Supplies the published comparison value for worked example 1: total mean mass of the atmosphere 5.1480 x 10^18 kg, dry air mass 5.1352 +/- 0.0003 x 10^18 kg, global mean total surface pressure 985.50 hPa, from ERA-40 data 1979-2001. sourceRecords.notes: Page as read on 2026-08-19 states that in 2023 U.S. finished motor gasoline consumption averaged about 8.94 million barrels per day, about 376 million gallons per day, with 42 U.S. gallons per barrel, and that the record was about 392 million gallons per day in 2018; page last updated March 29, 2024 with Petroleum Supply Monthly data. sourceRecords.title: Trinity revisited (National Security Science, Los Alamos National Laboratory)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the previously accepted 21-kiloton Trinity yield and the 2021 reassessment of about 24.8 kilotons by Hugh Selby and colleagues in the Laboratory's nuclear and radiochemistry group, using inorganic separations chemistry and high-precision mass spectrometry on trinitite samples.

sourceRecords.title: Fermi at Trinity (Nuclear Technology 207, S326, 2021)
sourceRecords.provider: American Nuclear Society / J. I. Katz (Washington University in St. Louis)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the arXiv abstract page for the open preprint of the Nuclear Technology article. Confirms that Fermi estimated the Trinity yield by dropping small pieces of paper and observing their motion in the blast wave, that his figure was about 10 kilotons, that this is roughly 40 percent of the accepted radiochemical value of 25 +/- 2 kilotons, and that the shortfall is expected because the blast wave excludes the thermal and nuclear-radiation share of the energy. The paper reconstructs the analysis Fermi is likely to have used, which had not previously been documented. No text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.5.5.2: Formulas for functions of two variables
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology / SEMATECH
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the statement that for a product of independent quantities the relative standard deviation is the quadrature sum of the relative standard deviations, and that a covariance term must be added when the factors are correlated. Used to justify the quadrature argument in the lesson and to bound its validity.

sourceRecords.title: Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide: Best Practices for Developing and Managing Program Costs (GAO-20-195G, March 2020)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the GAO product page and extracted text from the full PDF copy hosted at https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-08/gao-20-195g.pdf. Confirms the four characteristics of a reliable estimate (comprehensive, well documented, accurate, credible), the 18 best practices, the 12-step process, Chapter 8 / Step 5 'Identify Ground Rules and Assumptions', and the statement that element-specific ground rules and assumptions carry the most uncertainty and must be checked for realism and well documented for the estimate to be considered credible. Supports the professional obligation to label an estimate and record its assumptions.
